source_title: From Hitler to India’s farmers: How Great Depression changed lives beyond US
source_excerpt: In October 1929, billions of dollars in wealth evaporated from the American stock market, setting off an economic catastrophe that would reach far beyond Wall Street.Years of speculative buying, easy credit and inflated share prices had created a market built on the expectation that stocks would keep rising. When confidence collapsed, investors rushed to sell. The Dow Jones Industrial Average plunged nearly 13 per cent on October 28 and another 12 per cent the following day, in what became known as Black Monday and Black Tuesday.But the crash was only the beginning. Bank failures, collapsing demand and business closures deepened the American downturn, while the withdrawal of US loans, falling international trade and the constraints of the gold standard carried the crisis across borders.The result was the Great Depression, a global disaster that would help propel Adolf Hitler towards power in Germany, devastate farmers in colonial India, push millions of Britons into unemployment, and expose the fragility of economies around the world.What followed was not merely a financial collapse, but a decade of economic hardship and political upheaval that changed the course of the twentieth century.Germanyâs economic collapse turned Hitler into a political forceThe Great Depression hit Germany at a time when its economy was already vulnerable, turning a global financial crisis into a national catastrophe. The country was still struggling with the consequences of the First World War, including reparations, political instability and the devastating hyperinflation of 1923.Its recovery during the second half of the 1920s depended heavily on foreign credit, particularly loans from the United States.Under the Dawes Plan of 1924, American lending helped stabilise German finances and supported economic recovery. But this dependence became a major weakness when the Wall Street crash struck in October 1929.As American banks and investors came under pressure, new lending dried up and foreign creditors recalled short-term loans. German banks and businesses struggled to obtain credit, investment declined and companies began cutting production and jobs.The consequences were severe. Industrial output contracted, businesses failed and unemployment soared. By 1932, around 5.6 million Germans were registered as unemployed, while industrial production had fallen by approximately 40 per cent from its 1928 level.The crisis also paralysed political decision-making. Chancellor Hermann MÃ¼llerâs coalition government collapsed in March 1930 amid disagreements over unemployment insurance, paving the way for increasingly unstable governments that relied on presidential emergency powers.This economic desperation created an opening for Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party. They portrayed the Weimar Republic as weak and incapable of protecting ordinary Germans, promising jobs, national revival and decisive leadership. Their message appealed to sections of the middle class, struggling farmers, small business owners and workers disillusioned with the political establishment.The electoral shift was dramatic. According to the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, the Nazis won just 2.6 per cent of the vote in the 1928 parliamentary election. Their share rose to 18 per cent in September 1930 and 37 per cent in July 1932, making them the largest party in the Reichstag.Nazi campaigning deliberately exploited the hardship. A 1932 election poster preserved by the US Holocaust Memorial Museum carried the slogan âOur Last Hope - Hitlerâ, presenting the Nazi leader as an answer to national despair.The party used mass rallies, newspapers, posters and speeches to promise economic recovery and political order. At the same time, it spread antisemitic conspiracy theories, blamed Jews and communists for Germanyâs problems, and attacked democratic institutions.Hitler did not win an outright majority in a free national election. On January 30, 1933, President Paul von Hindenburg appointed him chancellor following negotiations with conservative political leaders who believed they could control him. The Nazis subsequently dismantled democracy and established a dictatorship.The Great Depression did not, by itself, cause Hitlerâs rise. But the collapse of American lending, mass unemployment and the failure of Germanyâs political leadership to restore confidence created conditions that the Nazis exploited with devastating consequences.Indiaâs farmers were crushed as crop prices collapsedIn British-ruled India, the Great Depression turned a global economic crisis into a rural emergency, exposing the financial vulnerability of millions of cultivators and deepening resentment against colonial rule.As international demand weakened and agricultural prices plunged, farmers earned less from their crops but continued to face debts, rent and land revenue obligations. For many, the crisis meant selling produce at a loss, struggling to repay moneylenders and risking the loss of their land.A 2022 research paper by historian Alok Oak, published in Studies in Indian Politics, documents the scale of the collapse. Indiaâs agricultural price index fell from 203 in 1929 to 127 in 1931, using 1873 as the base year. The price index for raw cotton dropped from 133 to 70 over the same period. The decline was particularly damaging for cultivators who depended on commercial crops to generate cash for household expenses, rent and taxes.The crisis was compounded by the structure of the colonial economy. According to Oak, the British government refused to devalue the rupee amid concerns about meeting its foreign financial obligations. Meanwhile, Britainâs exports to India fell from Â£90.6 million in 1924 to Â£52.9 million in 1930, a decline of about 41 per cent. Falling trade and agricultural prices squeezed rural incomes and weakened economic activity.The timing was significant for Indiaâs independence movement. At its Lahore session in December 1929, the Indian National Congress declared Purna Swaraj, or complete independence, as its goal. On January 26, 1930, Congress observed Independence Day, building momentum for a new phase of resistance.The Depression did not create the struggle against British rule, which had much deeper roots, but worsening economic conditions made questions of taxation, rural livelihoods and control over Indiaâs economy more urgent.Mahatma Gandhi launched the Civil Disobedience Movement in 1930, beginning with the Salt March from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi. By challenging the British monopoly on salt and the tax imposed on a basic necessity, Gandhi chose an issue that affected Indians across social and economic divisions. The campaign transformed an everyday grievance into an act of mass resistance and helped bring the nationalist movement into the lives of ordinary people.Gandhi also urged Indians to boycott foreign goods, particularly British-made cloth, and promoted khadi and domestic production. These campaigns had a political and economic purpose. Reducing dependence on imported goods could challenge British commercial interests while encouraging Indians to support local producers. At a time when the global crisis had exposed the vulnerability of export-dependent economies, the message of economic self-reliance gained added significanceResearch by Stanford University political scientists Rikhil Bhavnani and Saumitra Jha has also identified a link between economic shocks and nationalist mobilisation. Their working paper found that districts producing export crops and affected by interwar trade shocks, including the Depression, were more likely to support the independence movement in the 1937 and 1946 elections.The researchers argue that these shocks helped bring agricultural exporters into a broader coalition demanding political change. The findings suggest that the Depressionâs political consequences extended beyond immediate protests and influenced support for nationalism in subsequent years.The crisis also reinforced Gandhiâs emphasis on village industries and economic self-reliance. He argued that political freedom would mean little if rural India remained trapped in poverty and dependent on external markets. Gandhi promoted khadi and cottage industries as ways to create employment, strengthen village economies and reduce dependence on imported goods.In 1934, the All-India Village Industries Association was established to advance this wider effort. Historian Alok Oak argues that the Depression and the limits of colonial economic policy helped strengthen Gandhiâs focus on rural production and economic autonomy.Britainâs industrial decline pushed millions out of workBritain entered the Great Depression with its traditional industries already struggling to compete in international markets. Coal mining, shipbuilding, iron and textiles faced declining demand and growing competition, leaving industrial communities vulnerable when the Wall Street crash of 1929 further restricted global trade.As exports weakened and businesses cut production, unemployment soared. According to the UK National Archives, the number of unemployed people climbed to almost 3.5 million by 1932, with the North East of England, Scotlandâs industrial lowlands and the mining valleys of Wales among the hardest-hit regions.Families faced prolonged hardship, while the governmentâs introduction of a means test in 1931 intensified resentment among people seeking unemployment assistance.The crisis also exposed the limits of Britainâs monetary policy. The country had returned to the gold standard in 1925, tying sterling to a fixed gold value. As economic activity contracted, deflation deepened and unemployment rose, the government faced growing pressure to defend the pound while supporting the domestic economy.The situation became critical in 1931 as investors withdrew funds from London and the Bank of England lost gold reserves. The National Archivesâ record of the governmentâs September 20 announcement says more than Â£200 million had been withdrawn from the London market since mid-July. Britain suspended the gold standard the following day.The political consequences were immediate. The Labour government under Ramsay MacDonald split over how to address the financial emergency and public spending. MacDonald subsequently formed a National Government with Conservative and Liberal support, while Labour suffered a major defeat in the October 1931 election.The departure from gold eventually gave Britain greater freedom to lower interest rates and allowed sterling to depreciate, helping exporters and supporting the early stages of recovery.A research paper by economists Jason Lennard and Meredith M Paker found that leaving the gold standard reduced unemployment by 2.7 percentage points in export-intensive industries relative to less export-dependent industries.Yet recovery was uneven. Traditional industrial regions continued to experience hardship, and hunger marches brought the plight of unemployed workers into public view.Britainâs experience demonstrated how the Great Depression could undermine established industries, destabilise governments and force a major economic power to abandon a monetary system it had once considered essential to financial stability.From Wall Street to the WorldThe Great Depression proved that an economic crisis does not stop at a countryâs borders. A stock market collapse in America helped fuel the rise of Hitler in Germany, deepened the misery of farmers in colonial India, pushed millions of Britons out of work, and devastated economies around the world.Yet the damage went far beyond lost jobs, failed banks and falling crop prices. Across continents, the Depression changed not only how people earned a living, but also how they viewed their governments and their future.Its legacy helped reshape the global economic order. The failure of protectionism, the instability of international finance and the inability of countries to contain the crisis through isolated national responses influenced the push for greater economic cooperation after the Second World War, including the Bretton Woods system.But the Depressionâs most enduring warning is political as much as economic: when livelihoods collapse and governments appear powerless, public anger can become an opening for extremism.The crash began on Wall Street in 1929; its consequences reached farms, factories, homes and parliaments around the world, changing the course of the twentieth century.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
